newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak daily to appeal government libel verdict.
newsitem.headline: Slovak daily to appeal government libel verdict.

text.p: The Slovak independent daily Sme said on Thursday it would appeal against a court ruling ordering it to pay a large fine for a story accusing the government of involvement in a politically-charged murder case.

A district court ordered Sme on Wednesday to pay damages of 7.5 million Slovak crowns ($250,000) to ministers because it said their individual rights were violated in a story saying the government bore responsibility for a former policeman's death.
The court in the central city of Banska Bystrica also ordered Sme to issue an apology to the 18-member cabinet.
The fines include 500,000 crowns to be paid to Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, 450,000 each to his three deputy premiers, and 400,000 each to the other members.
"We will appeal against the verdict," Svetlana Kolesarova, deputy editor-in-chief, told Reuters.
Kolesarova said Sme, one of the newspapers most critical of Meciar and his government, would issue a statement on the affair after consulting its lawyers.

The government sued both Sme's publisher and investigative journalist Peter Toth for linking it to the murder of Robert Remias, an ex-policeman who became a key figure in the probe of the kidnapping of the president's adult son Michal Kovac Jr.
Toth, speaking at Remias's funeral, described Remias as the first victim "of a cold war carried out by the government against its citizens". The comment was carried in a Sme story.

The court said Sme's article reporting on the comment had directly tied the government to Remias's death, but the court rejected the government's charge against Toth, saying he had not directly accused the government of committing a crime.
Kolesarova said the appeal would be sought in Kosice, eastern Slovakia, to avoid bias because Banska Bystrice is a Meciar stronghold.
Remias was killed last April when his car exploded on the outskirts of Bratislava. Police said the blast was caused by an explosive device placed in the car.
Remias acted as a go-between for the media for a close friend and former officer of the Slovak secret service SIS who claimed to have taken part in the kidnapping.
The officer, now in hiding, said the kidnapping was organised and carried out by the SIS on the orders of its director and close Meciar ally Ivan Lexa.
Kovak Junior was seized near Bratislava on August 31, 1995, bundled into the boot of his car and dumped outside a police station 10 km (six miles) inside neigbouring Austria.
He was detained in Austria to face extradition to Germany on suspicion of fraud but a Vienna court later freed him.

The opposition alleges that the kidnapping was engineered to compromise President Kovac. The president was instrumental in Meciar's dismissal as premier in the spring of 1994 by calling on parliament to pass a no-confidence vote.
Two veteran detectives were taken off the case after their investigations led them to the SIS. A third suspended the case for lack of evidence. The Remias case was also shelved on the same grounds.
Earlier this year Sme was forced to change to a printer some 100 km (62 miles) outside Bratislava after its regular printer revoked its contract. Sme said this was a result of outside pressure.
The Slovak government has been repeatedly warned by the European Union and the United States for adopting anti-democratic measures which they say could threaten chances of NATO and EU membership.
